Why you should never, ever, ever use MongoDB

TL;DR:

Never use a database because 'everybody else does', do your own research as to the advantages and drawbacks of a particular database.

The trendiness of Mongo is a great illustration of the worst parts of the culture of this industry: brogrammers with zero attention spans constantly flocking from one "cool" new technology to another, never pausing long enough to question whether said technology is appropriate for the job, or reliable, or secure. I love web development (and a lot of aspects of its culture) but the herd mentality is going to result in some serious consequences one day.
I use mysql / MariaDB and have had good luck with it. Postgre has been the leading alternative for years but I haven't used it on a project.

But its web scale...

I used it on one small project & didn't have any issues. Selfishly I'd rather not use any database that doesn't have native support within SQLAlchemy. My past few projects have used Postgres & SQLite.
MongoDB is the Ruby of databases. You don't use it because it's a good idea. You use it because you are a lazy hipster.

I played with Mongo for few weeks, I never really liked new technologies when dealing with data storage, I still have to find a good solution to databases like Postgres, MySQL, Cassandra and Elastic Search... All these 4 have a long history and are widely used in different domains, I tried to port some web apps using a SQL oriented database to MongoDB, the result was absolutely horrendum! Tuned PostgreSQL outperformed tuned MongoDB by almost an order of magnitude for some queries, and after few days started to freak out due to the amount of data to handle.

Even if I am relative young as developer, I never felt the necessity to find a new technology when dealing with data storage, old proved solutions are still the best choice, at least they don't lose data... :)

Good lord folks, have you even tried it? There are stellar use cases for MongoDB, and if you'd read the first page of docs you'd avoid damn near all of the complaints about it. This whole thread stinks of Ludditism. Yes, relational data is better stored in a relational database, but that's pretty much where the argument ends. Gnarly JSON-shaped data eats join optimizers for breakfast; Mongo excels there. Different jobs, different tools.

I have been using iOS for nearly 6 years now and am looking to make the switch to Android. About three years ago, in a painkiller induced spending spree, I purchased the Samsung Galaxy S4 (literally, after a surgery). I regretted the purchase and sold the phone shortly after getting it for a variety of reasons. I put together a list of things that I would need out of an Android phone to make the switch again and was hoping someone here could point me in the right direction:

  1. No gimmicks: The S4 had a terrible suite of software such as eye tracking and other voice commands that never worked. They slowed the phone down and served no real purpose for me personally.

  2. Minimal bloatware: In this day and age it is near impossible to find a phone without bloatware, as even iPhones come loaded with Apple software one might not need. The S4 took this to a whole different level though. Samsung and Verizon software clogged the thing up so bad I couldn't think straight looking in the app drawer. I have since switched to T-Mobile. Something closest to stock Android would be ideal, like a Google edition phone.

  3. Metal or leather casing (no external case ideally needed but not necessary): The S4 was a chunk of plastic that was covered in nicks and dents after a couple weeks, no bueno.

  4. Fingerprint reader: This is not a necessity, but definitely preferred as I was spoiled with the 5S.

  5. Modern hardware: Not trying to spend money on an outdated phone obviously.

Some of you might be thinking at this point "What's the big deal, just put a custom ROM on the phone, or get a leather case, or turn the gimmicky software off". Although I agree to some extent, I am old and don't have time to constantly be messing with ROMs, tweaks, etc. So are there any phones out there that sort of describe what I am looking for? A Google search shows so many options it is hard to know what is decent as of 2015. Thanks!

  5. Nexus phones will get you the best hardware for the money (the cameras are usually not up to par with iPhones, but the Nexus 6 changed that)

If you can get past the no metal/leather casing and no fingerprint reader, Nexus phones are your best choice if you care about not having bloatware.
